procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated October 30, 1970, of the Jammu and Kashmir High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 12 of 1969 and Criminal Reference No. 10 of 1969, which dismissed the appellant's appeal and confirmed the sentence of death.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant was convicted of murder by the Sessions Court and sentenced to death. The case then went to the High Court as a criminal appeal by the appellant and as a murder reference for confirmation of the death sentence. The High Court examined a ballistic expert and permitted the appellant to examine another ballistic expert (Siyaram Gupta) and two other witnesses (Shri Ratan Sahgal and C. L. Wasan). C. L. Wasan was allowed to be examined even though he had already been examined earlier as a prosecution witness. The High Court declined the appellant's request to produce more defense witnesses. Ultimately, the High Court dismissed the appeal and confirmed the death sentence. An oral prayer for a certificate to appeal to the Supreme Court was declined.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's judgment and order. The Supreme Court limited the arguments to two points, stating that if they agreed with the appellant on those points, the appeal would succeed and the appellant would be acquitted. The Supreme Court noted that the High Court appeared to have disregarded legal processes and failed to consider vital aspects, causing serious prejudice to the appellant, resulting in grave and substantial injustice.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in using statements recorded under Section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) to corroborate the testimony of witnesses in court.

facts: The High Court relied on statements made by various witnesses to the police during the investigation, recorded under Section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.).
The High Court used these S.161 statements to find corroboration for the testimony the same witnesses later gave in court.

Specifically, the High Court used the S.161 statements to support the witnesses' claim that they had disclosed the accused's name to the police, a fact that was missing from the First Information Report (F.I.R.).
law: The Supreme Court cited Section 162 of the Cr.P.C., stating that its language is "plain and explicit."
Section 162 Cr.P.C. prohibits a court from using statements made to the police during an investigation (under S.161) for the purpose of corroborating the statements made by those witnesses in court.
The law provides a restricted and specific use for such statements, primarily for the accused to contradict a witness, not for the prosecution or the court to use as corroborative evidence.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had committed a clear error by using the S.161 statements for a purpose expressly forbidden by law.

The Court stated, "The High Court was clearly in error in taking into consideration the contents of the statement recorded under s. 161, Cr. P.C. during the course of inves'tigation for the purpose of finding corroboration of the statements made in court."
The Supreme Court noted that the High Court had repeatedly made this error with the statements of a large number of witnesses.
By excluding the improperly considered S.161 statements, the Supreme Court found there was no reliable material left on the record to sustain the appellant's conviction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the High Court had erred. It held that under Section 162 of the Cr.P.C., statements recorded by the police during an investigation cannot be used to corroborate the testimony of witnesses in court. Since the High Court had improperly relied on this legally inadmissible corroboration to convict the appellant, the Supreme Court overturned the conviction and acquitted the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was sufficient legal evidence on record to sustain the appellant's conviction for murder and other offences, particularly concerning the identification of the appellant.

facts: The appellant was convicted of murder by shooting, and the conviction was confirmed by the High Court.
The primary issue was the identification of the appellant as the person who fired the shots.
A key witness, Abdul Ghani Sheikh, identified the appellant for the first time in the Sessions Court.
This witness had not provided any description of the assailant in the initial police report (F.I.R.).
No test identification parade was ever conducted for the witnesses to identify the accused before the trial.
The High Court had relied on statements made by witnesses to the police under s. 161, Cr. P.C. to corroborate their testimony in court.
law: The substantive evidence of a witness is their testimony given in court.
When an accused person is not previously known to a witness, a test identification parade is an important piece of corroborating evidence.
Statements made to the police during an investigation under s. 161, Cr. P.C. are not admissible to corroborate a witness's testimony in court.
application: The Court found the in-court identification of the appellant to be a "far too slender a piece of evidence" to support a conviction.
The Court reasoned that this identification was unreliable because it was not supported by any prior identification at a test parade or by any description of the assailant in the F.I.R.
The Court held that the High Court had erred in law by using inadmissible statements made to the police (under s. 161, Cr. P.C.) to support the conviction.

After excluding the inadmissible police statements and finding the in-court identification evidence to be insufficient and unreliable, the Court was left with no credible material to uphold the conviction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that there was no reliable legal evidence on record to sustain the appellant's conviction. It found the High Court was in error, allowed the appeal, and acquitted the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in using statements recorded under Section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) to corroborate the testimony of witnesses in court.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was in error to use statements recorded by police under Section 161, Cr.P.C. for the purpose of corroborating the testimony of witnesses given in court.
Under Section 162, Cr.P.C., such statements can only be used to contradict a witness, not to support or corroborate their testimony.
respondent_arguments: The statements recorded under Section 161 Cr.P.C. were used to prove that the eyewitnesses had disclosed the appellant's name to the police soon after the FIR was lodged.
This was necessary to counter the defense's claim that the naming of the appellant was a belated invention, as the name was not mentioned in the initial FIR.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there was sufficient legal evidence on record to sustain the appellant's conviction for murder and other offences, particularly concerning the identification of the appellant.
appellant_arguments: The identification of the appellant was not proven, as his name was not mentioned in the First Information Report (FIR).
The failure of the investigating authorities to arrest the appellant immediately after the incident casts doubt on the claim that his name was disclosed by witnesses at that time.
No test identification parade was conducted to confirm the identity of the appellant.
Once the inadmissible evidence (statements under S. 161 Cr.P.C.) is excluded, there is no reliable material left to sustain the conviction.
respondent_arguments: The omission of the appellant's name from the FIR is not sufficient to demolish the prosecution's case.
The failure to mention the name in the FIR was a matter of 'minute detail' that may have been overlooked because the report was lodged immediately after the occurrence.
The eyewitnesses had clearly stated the appellant's name in their statements to the police shortly after the FIR was filed, proving that his identity was known from the beginning.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A statement recorded by the police under Section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code cannot be used for the purpose of corroborating the statements made by a witness in court. The use of such a statement is explicitly limited by Section 162 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which only permits its use to contradict a witness as provided by Section 145 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
obiter: It is not necessary to refer to a large catena of decisions reported in law reports and cited in text-books stating the legal position with regard to the restricted use of such statements.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Once the inadmissible statements made under Section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code are excluded from consideration, and in the absence of a test identification parade, there is no reliable material on the record upon which the appellant's conviction can be sustained.
legal_tests_applied: Section 162 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) establishes the limited use of statements made to the police during an investigation (under S. 161), explicitly prohibiting their use to corroborate the testimony of witnesses in court; such statements can only be used for contradiction.

The court's scrutiny of evidence must include the manner in which the investigation was conducted, including omissions like the failure of investigating authorities to take prompt action based on alleged information.
policy_considerations: Courts must not disregard the established forms of legal process, as doing so can cause serious prejudice to the accused and result in grave and substantial injustice.

A failure by the High Court to advert to important and vital aspects of the case, such as the investigating authorities' inaction after the alleged disclosure of a suspect's name, is a serious error that can undermine a conviction.
